subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Draw the sky as it appears in the morning, afternoon, and at night (p. 152)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quick whole-class oral warm-up: 'Close your eyes and picture the sky right now — what colour is it? What would it look like at midnight?' Children share words aloud, no writing yet, just gathering mental images.

Students open Textbook p. 152 and look at the three blank panels. The teacher names each panel — morning, afternoon, night — and asks children to whisper what they expect to see in each before drawing anything.

Children draw their three sky pictures independently: morning (colour, Sun, perhaps birds or a faint Moon), afternoon (brightest blue or white haze, Sun high), night (dark sky, Moon in one of its shapes, stars). They add small labels or colour notes beside each panel.

A gallery pause: children hold up or pass their books to a neighbour. The teacher invites two or three volunteers to name one detail in their drawing that they are most sure of, and one they are less sure about — seeding honest observation before the next round of sky-watching.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent observed features of a natural phenomenon at different times of day through labelled drawings.
periods.section_context: Sky colour changes from morning to afternoon to night, Sun's apparent colour and brightness, Moon's visible shape at night, stars.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did everyone draw the same colour sky for morning — or are there differences? Why might that be?' Draw out that personal observation times and weather vary; there is no single wrong answer. If children mention the Sun's colour, gently prompt: 'Have you ever seen the Sun look orange or red — when does that happen?' — this surfaces awareness of sunrise and sunset hues without telling.

periods.activity_title: Sky Observation Table: Filling What We Notice
periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Record observations of the sky during morning, afternoon, and night in the table given (p. 153)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the partially filled observation table on Textbook p. 153, pausing at each pre-filled example to ask, 'Has anyone actually noticed this?' Children indicate with a thumbs-up or thumbs-down, getting them to evaluate observations rather than just copy.

Children complete the unfilled cells of the table using what they recall from real experience and from the drawings they made. They then add at least two new rows of their own — details the printed table did not mention, such as changes in wind, temperature feel, or the presence of clouds and fog.

Pair share (Textbook p. 153 discussion prompt): each child reads one of their self-added rows to a partner. Partners decide whether the observation fits morning, afternoon, or night — or all three — and mark it accordingly. The teacher circulates, listening for unexpected but valid observations.

Whole-class share: the teacher collects two or three surprising additions on the board. The class votes on which sky-time they belong to, consolidating that the sky is a complex, changing scene, not just bright or dark.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically record and categorise observations of a natural phenomenon across different conditions.
periods.section_context: Sky colour and brightness at morning, afternoon, night; Sun's visibility and brightness; presence of Moon and stars; changes in clouds and atmosphere across the day.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Your neighbour added a row you did not — does that mean one of you was wrong?' Guide children to see that different people observe at different times and places; both can be right. If a child mentions that animals or plants also change, validate and link to the next discussion prompt in the textbook — but let it arise from children, not the teacher.

periods.activity_title: Sunrise, Sunset: Sharing What We've Seen
periods.textbook_anchor: Pictures of the Sky — Discuss changes observed at sunrise and sunset including sky appearance, animal behaviour, and changes at home (p. 154)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: two columns labelled Sunrise and Sunset for class contributions

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a simple two-column table on the board: Sunrise | Sunset. Children are asked to silently recall one thing they have personally seen at sunrise (or early morning) and one at sunset, then share aloud. The teacher scribes contributions without evaluation.

Students open Textbook p. 154 and work through the three sub-questions for both sunrise and sunset: sky appearance, bird and animal behaviour, changes at home. They discuss in small groups of three, with one child scribing the group's ideas in their notebook.

Groups report back one observation each. The teacher highlights patterns that emerge across groups: lights being switched on at dusk, birds going quiet, flowers closing — connecting animal and plant behaviour to sky changes, as the section prompts. Traditional morning and evening routines mentioned by children (lamps lit, prayers, milking of cows) are welcomed as real-life data.

Brief reflection: children write one sentence in their notebooks completing the stem — 'At sunrise the sky _______ and at sunset the sky _______.' This anchors the discussion in a personal written record.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect changes in a natural phenomenon to observable changes in living things and daily human routines.
periods.section_context: Sunrise and sunset sky appearance, bird and animal behaviour at sunrise and sunset, changes in home routines at sunrise and sunset.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does everyone at home do the same things at sunrise — or does it depend on your family's work or habits?' This opens space for diversity in daily rhythms without privileging any one routine. If children mention lamps, azan, temple bells, or farm work beginning, affirm these as real-world sky-linked events.

periods.activity_title: Torch and Stick: Investigating Shadow Formation
periods.textbook_anchor: The Shadows — Observe shadow changes when a stick is moved back and forth and when the torch direction is changed in a darkened room (p. 156)
materials: straight stick or pencil (one per group)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses a question without answering it: 'Your shadow at school in the morning points one way; at noon it almost disappears. What could be causing that?' Children guess aloud. The teacher lists guesses on the board and says the class will test one of them.

Groups of four darken their workspace as much as possible (curtains drawn, doors adjusted). They read the setup from Textbook p. 156 — torch on, stick held upright — and observe the basic shadow before any changes are made. One child sketches the shadow's rough shape and direction in the notebook.

Groups work through both investigations: (a) move the stick closer to and farther from the torch — observe shadow size change; (b) tilt or redirect the torch — observe shadow direction change. Children draw two sketches for each situation: one with the stick near, one far; one torch direction, another. They label what changed.

Groups share findings aloud. The teacher asks: 'Which guess from the board did our experiment support?' Children connect torch position to Sun position and explain why shadows are long in the morning and short at noon in their own words.
Children write one sentence: 'The shadow gets _______ when the light source is _______ the object.' — a close-the-loop record of the causal relationship discovered.

periods.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple investigation to identify causal relationships between a light source's position and the size and direction of shadows.
periods.section_context: Shadow size change when stick is moved toward and away from torch, shadow direction change when torch direction changes, torch as model of Sun.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why did we use a torch instead of the real Sun? What are the advantages and limitations of our experiment?' This prompts children to think about the investigation itself, not just the result. If groups get different results because of different room brightness, treat it as real inquiry data: 'Why might two groups get different shadow sizes?'

periods.activity_title: Shadow Drawing: Sun Position and Shadow Direction
periods.textbook_anchor: The Shadows — Draw the position of the Sun and corresponding shadows in the images given (p. 157)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure on p. 157 showing silhouette diagrams for shadow drawing

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a simple stick figure on the board and asks: 'If the Sun is on this side at morning, where does the shadow fall?' A child comes up and draws the shadow. The class checks and adjusts. The teacher repeats for noon and late afternoon, letting children come up each time — making the rule visible before the textbook task.

Students open Textbook p. 157 and complete the shadow-drawing task: for each diagram they draw (a) the Sun in its correct position for that time of day and (b) the shadow of the figure in the correct direction and approximate length. They use a ruler to keep shadow lines straight. Morning = long shadow opposite the Sun; noon = short shadow nearly underfoot; afternoon = long shadow on the opposite side from morning.

Children exchange books with a partner. Partners check each diagram using the rule they articulated in the opening. If a shadow points in the wrong direction, the partner circles it and writes a question mark — no red-pen corrections, only flags for discussion.

Brief class discussion: the teacher asks two pairs to share a disagreement they had. The class resolves it together, reinforcing the directional rule. The teacher connects to the cultural note — that ancient people noticed exactly this pattern and built structures to read time from it, such as the Jantar Mantar observatories and the Samrat Yantra — drawing it naturally from what children have just drawn.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent the relationship between a light source's position and shadow direction and length through labelled diagrams.
periods.section_context: Sun position at morning, noon, and afternoon; shadow direction and length at each time; Jantar Mantar and Samrat Yantra as instruments that read time from shadows.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you could only look at your shadow — without looking at the sky — could you figure out roughly what time of day it is? How?' This takes children from drawing to reasoning. Mention that Raja Jai Singh's observatories did exactly this at a grand scale; invite children to share if anyone has visited Jaipur or seen pictures of Jantar Mantar.

periods.activity_title: Star Patterns and Moon Shapes: Observing the Night Sky
periods.textbook_anchor: Night Sky — Observe the Moon and draw the shapes of the Moon observed on different nights (p. 160)
materials: reference image of Saptarshi pattern (if available)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of star patterns including Saptarshi (p. 160 area); board sketch of Saptarshi dot pattern

time_bands.activity: The teacher dims lights if possible and asks children to shut their eyes and imagine the night sky they last saw. 'How many stars could you count? Did you see the Moon? What shape was it?' Children open their eyes and share. The teacher sketches three or four different Moon shapes on the board: full circle, half, crescent, absent.

Children open Textbook p. 160 and examine the Moon-shape drawing task. They draw at least four Moon shapes they have personally seen on different nights — or shapes they recognise from the textbook's examples. Under each shape they write a brief note: 'big and bright', 'thin like a banana', 'could not see it'. The teacher introduces the names Poornima and Amavasya from the text and asks if children have heard these words before.

The teacher draws the Saptarshi (Seven Sages) star pattern on the board as seven dots connected by lines. Children try to replicate it in their notebooks and discuss: 'Have you ever spotted a pattern like this in the night sky?' The teacher explains that ancient people across India and the world named star patterns and used them for navigation and storytelling.

Whole-class discussion on the two textbook prompts (p. 160): Is there a pattern to how the Moon's shape changes? Are there nights when the Moon is invisible? Children share yes/no with reasoning; the teacher charts the responses and affirms that the Moon follows a regular cycle — confirming the pattern children may have guessed.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe, name, and record repeating patterns in the appearance of celestial objects across different nights.
periods.section_context: Moon shapes (Poornima, half-moon, crescent, Amavasya/invisible), star patterns, Saptarshi constellation, twinkling stars.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family told you a story about the stars or given a group of stars a name? Share it.' This surfaces oral traditions and regional star-lore naturally. If children name non-Saptarshi patterns or folk names, write them on the board alongside — validating that sky observation is a human universal, not just a school activity.

periods.activity_title: Moon, Festivals, and Calendars: Connecting Sky to Culture
periods.textbook_anchor: Night Sky — Write about festivals in your family or community related to the Sun or Moon and what you call them in your language (p. 162)
periods.visual_aids: Board table: Moon Phase | Festival Name | Community / Language

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws the board table and fills in one example: Poornima | Guru Poornima | Hindi. Children are invited to fill in the next row from their own knowledge. The teacher asks: 'Why do you think so many festivals happen on a full Moon or a new Moon night?' Answers are collected without evaluation.

Children work on the Textbook p. 162 task: they write the name of at least one festival their family celebrates that is tied to the Moon or the Sun, the Moon phase on which it falls, and what it is called in their home language. They may ask neighbours quietly if they want to add more. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'When is Diwali — full Moon or no Moon? How do you know?'

Class share: each child reads out one festival name and the Moon phase. The teacher fills the board table as children speak. The class notices: some phases have many festivals from different communities; Amavasya and Poornima appear most often. The teacher reads aloud the textbook's examples — Diwali on Amavasya, Eid on first crescent, Rakshabandhan on Poornima — to compare with the class's own list.

The teacher connects to the textbook point that Moon-phase observation gave rise to the earliest calendars. Children discuss: 'What would happen if you had no clock or calendar — how would you know what month it was?' A child writes one closing sentence: 'People used the Moon's shape to _______.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a natural phenomenon's observable pattern and cultural practices in their community.
periods.section_context: Moon phases (Poornima, Amavasya, first crescent), festivals (Diwali, Rakshabandhan, Guru Poornima, Buddha Poornima, Eid, Pongal, Chhath Puja, Karva Chauth), lunar calendar origins.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Two children named different festivals for the same Moon phase — does that mean one is wrong?' Guide the class to see that the same Moon serves many communities' calendars, and that naming in different languages is a strength, not a confusion. Treat every festival named — including those not in the textbook — as valid data.

periods.activity_title: Chandrayaan and Comparing Day and Night
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — Give two differences between day and night, sky in morning and evening, activities during day and at night for humans and animals (p. 162)
periods.visual_aids: Board: two-column comparison table (Day | Night) for class contributions

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly introduces the Chandrayaan connection from Textbook p. 162: India's Vikram Lander reached the Moon on 23 August 2023 and collected surface data. The teacher asks: 'What do you think the surface of the Moon looks like? Does it have day and night?' Children guess — this opens the day-and-night comparison naturally.

Children work through the Textbook p. 162 comparison task: they write two differences for each of the four pairs — (a) day and night, (b) morning and evening sky, (c) human activities by day and at night, (d) animal activities by day and at night. They write independently first, then compare with a partner to see if their pairs match or differ.

Class build: the teacher fills the board table from children's responses. For each pair, the teacher asks, 'Is there any difference your partner had that you did not?' — encouraging children to add to their own lists rather than compete. Human and animal behaviour differences are both collected; the dual strand (natural sky change and human/animal cultural response) surfaces through children's own words.

The teacher closes with: 'Vikram Lander is on the Moon right now. There is no atmosphere there — so what do you think the sky looks like from the Moon?' Children share; the teacher accepts all responses as hypotheses, not facts — modelling scientific curiosity.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically compare two states of a natural phenomenon and describe how living things respond differently to each.
periods.section_context: Day versus night differences, morning sky versus evening sky, human activities by day and at night, animal activities by day and at night, Chandrayaan mission and Vikram Lander (23 August 2023).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'You wrote that animals sleep at night — but do ALL animals sleep at night? Can you think of any that are awake at night and sleep during the day?' This prevents overgeneralisation and keeps observation honest. If children know about nocturnal animals from experience or stories, invite those examples.

periods.activity_title: Questioning the Sun's Movement and Explaining Shadows
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — Explain why the shadow changes direction and length between morning and afternoon when you stand at the same spot (p. 163)
periods.visual_aids: Board: simple diagram of a stick figure with Sun positions at morning and afternoon

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the Meera scenario from Textbook p. 162 aloud: a teacher says the Sun appears to move from East to West; Meera wants to ask questions. Children brainstorm questions Meera might ask — the teacher scribes them on the board without answering any. After several minutes, children read their lists and the class sorts the questions: 'Which are about what we can observe? Which are about why it happens?'

Children write their own list of at least two questions Meera could ask, as the task requires. They then attempt to answer their own questions using what they have learned about the Sun's apparent path — explicitly modelling the inquiry cycle: ask, then try to answer from evidence. Partners exchange and evaluate: 'Is this question answerable from what we observed, or does it need a scientist?'

Children work on the shadow explanation task from Textbook p. 163: standing at the same spot in the morning, the shadow points one way; in the afternoon, another way. They write an explanation and answer whether the length would be the same. The teacher's board diagram shows Sun left of figure (morning → shadow right) and Sun right of figure (afternoon → shadow left), letting children check their written logic against the visual.

Two or three children read their shadow explanations aloud. The class offers one word of affirmation and one suggested addition. The teacher consolidates: 'The Sun's apparent position drives both the direction and the length of every shadow — and that is the same principle the Jantar Mantar was built on.' — tying inquiry to heritage without a separate segment.

periods.implied_lo: Students can formulate questions about an observed natural pattern and construct evidence-based explanations for the pattern's effects.
periods.section_context: Meera's questions about the Sun's apparent East-to-West movement, shadow direction change between morning and afternoon at the same spot, shadow length comparison at morning versus afternoon.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Meera's teacher said the Sun appears to move — why did the teacher use the word appears? Is the Sun actually moving or does it look that way?' Do not provide the answer; let children wrestle with the distinction between apparent and actual motion. This is exactly the spirit of scientific questioning the task is cultivating.

periods.activity_title: Our Sky: Poem, Riddle, and Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: India's Chandrayaan Mission — Write a poem inspired by the beauty of the sky and complete the riddle (p. 163)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens by connecting the entire chapter's arc: the sky holds the blazing Sun that traces shadows from morning to night; stars that form patterns our ancestors named; a Moon whose shape changes in a cycle that shaped human calendars and festivals; and now a spacecraft that has landed on that Moon and sent back data. Children name any one thing from across these ideas that they found most surprising — a quick oral round with no evaluation.

The teacher reads the partial riddle from Textbook p. 163 aloud: 'Only one colour, but not one size / Appears with light, looks very nice.' Children write their own second couplet to complete the riddle and then write their answer. The riddle is deliberately open — multiple completions are valid.

Children write a short poem (four to eight lines) inspired by the beauty of the sky, drawing on any part of the chapter: the changing Sun, the shadows it casts, the star patterns of the night, the Moon's phases, a festival connected to the Moon, or the wonder of Chandrayaan. They may illustrate one line if they choose. The teacher circulates quietly, reading over shoulders and offering a quiet word of encouragement — no corrections at this stage.

Poem share: four or five children read their poems aloud (or show their illustration). After each, the class identifies which part of the sky the poem captured — Sun, shadows, stars, Moon, space — building a collective map of the chapter's themes through creative expression. Children whose poems are not read add a title to theirs and circle the sky element they chose.

Closing reflection: the teacher asks, 'Has the way you look at the sky changed after this chapter? What will you look for tonight?' One-word or one-phrase answers around the class. No writing — the chapter ends with the children looking outward, not inward at a page.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present understanding of natural phenomena and cultural connections through creative written and drawn expression.
periods.section_context: Sky-inspired poem, riddle completion, Sun's daily arc and shadow effects, Moon phases and lunar calendar, star patterns, Chandrayaan mission, festival connections to sky objects.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Your poem does not have to be perfectly scientific — but does it have to be honest? What does it mean for a poem about the sky to be honest?' This keeps creative expression tethered to real observation without stifling imagination. Accept poems in any language the child feels most fluent in — a poem in a home language about the Moon is as valid as one in English or Hindi.

assessment_items.task: In the three boxes below, draw what the sky looks like in the morning, in the afternoon, and at night. In each box, write two things you notice — about the colour, the Sun or Moon, or any stars. Label each box with the time of day.
assessment_items.scaffold: Box 1: Morning sky — draw and write two things you notice. Box 2: Afternoon sky — draw and write two things you notice. Box 3: Night sky — draw and write two things you notice.
format_of_output: Three labelled drawings with written observations
At least two written observations per box
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any accurate sky feature for each time: morning (reddish or orange sky, Sun near horizon, some stars fading, birds visible), afternoon (bright blue or white sky, Sun high, few or no clouds depending on region), night (dark sky, Moon in any phase, twinkling stars). Regional variation note: sky features such as haze, fog, or storm clouds vary by geography and season — accept all locally accurate descriptions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent observed features of a natural phenomenon at different times of day through labelled drawings.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the child can accurately recall and represent sky features across three distinct time periods, distinguishing colour, light source visibility, and celestial objects appropriate to each time.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each box prompts two written observations — look for specificity (not just 'bright') and correct placement of the Sun (morning: low; afternoon: high; night: absent). Drawings should reflect colour change and presence or absence of Moon and stars.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: distinct colours across three boxes, Sun correctly positioned or absent, Moon/stars appear only in night box, observations are specific ('orange sky', 'no stars'). Weak: identical sky in all three boxes, Sun drawn at night, no written observations added.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have not observed the sky at all three times may draw from memory or from the class discussion; accept plausible reasoning even without direct experience. Children who draw in regional styles are not penalised.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing with labels mirrors the textbook task and allows children of varying writing fluency to demonstrate observational knowledge through multiple modes simultaneously.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya fills in her sky observation table. For the morning column she writes: 'sky is bright blue, Sun is high up, no stars.' Which of her entries is incorrect?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. In the morning the Sun is near the horizon (low in the sky), not high up — it rises to overhead position only around noon. This tests accurate recording of the Sun's apparent position at a specific time.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically record and categorise observations of a natural phenomenon across different conditions.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'sky is bright blue' indicates the student does not distinguish between morning (which can be blue but also orange/pink near the horizon) and afternoon; it also suggests they may not have been precise in their table entries.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'no stars visible' suggests the student does not recognise that stars are indeed invisible in daylight — they may believe stars are only a night phenomenon that disappears rather than understanding the Sun's brightness outshines them.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'the Sun gives light' suggests the student is looking for a false statement and has confused a correct general fact with an incorrect observation entry — a reading-comprehension failure rather than a content failure.

assessment_items.question_text: Raju woke up early and noticed that birds were calling loudly, lights were being switched on at home, and the sky was changing colour. Write two changes that happen in the sky and two changes that happen with animals or at home during sunrise.
expected_elements: At least one accurate sky change at sunrise (e.g., sky turns orange or pink, Sun appears near the horizon, stars fade, it becomes lighter)
At least one additional sky change or a second valid sky observation at sunrise
At least one accurate animal or home change at sunrise (e.g., birds begin calling or flying, animals become active, lights are switched on, people wake up)
At least one further animal or home change at sunrise
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per clearly stated and accurate element, up to four marks. Regional variation note: specific bird species, home routines (prayer calls, milking, cooking) and sky colours at sunrise vary by geography — accept all locally accurate answers.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect changes in a natural phenomenon to observable changes in living things and daily human routines.

assessment_items.question_text: Ananya set up a torch and a stick in a darkened room. She moved the stick close to the torch and then far away from it. She also pointed the torch from different sides. Write two things she would observe about the shadow when she changed the stick's distance, and one thing she would observe when she changed the torch's direction.
expected_elements: When the stick is moved close to the torch, the shadow becomes larger (or bigger)
When the stick is moved far from the torch, the shadow becomes smaller
When the torch direction is changed, the shadow direction also changes (shadow moves to the opposite side of the light)
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per element. Full marks require all three elements. A student who states size changes without specifying direction (larger/smaller) earns partial credit for that element only if the size change is directionally correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can perform a simple investigation to identify causal relationships between a light source's position and the size and direction of shadows.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: When the stick is moved close to the torch, the shadow becomes larger (or bigger)
When the stick is moved far from the torch, the shadow becomes smaller
When the torch direction is changed, the shadow direction also changes (shadow moves to the opposite side of the light)

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the diagram below. A child stands upright and the Sun is to her right. In which direction will her shadow fall?

Sun → [Child figure] ___?___

options.label: A
options.text: Behind her, away from both Sun and child

options.label: B
options.text: Directly below her feet, straight down

options.label: C
options.text: To the left, opposite to the Sun

options.label: D
options.text: To the right, same side as the Sun

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. The shadow always falls on the side opposite the light source. This tests the core directional rule of shadow formation that the textbook drawing activity established.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent the relationship between a light source's position and shadow direction and length through labelled diagrams.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'to the right, same side as the Sun' indicates the student believes the shadow follows the light rather than opposing it — a fundamental misconception about shadow formation that the torch investigation was designed to address.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'directly below her feet' suggests the student conflates noon shadow behaviour (when the Sun is directly overhead) with any Sun position — failing to apply the directional rule to lateral Sun positions.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'behind her, away from both Sun and child' indicates confusion between the direction a person faces and the direction of shadow fall — the student may be applying a forward/backward body-orientation frame rather than a light-source frame.

assessment_items.task: Draw the four shapes of the Moon that you have observed or learned about. Write the name of each shape next to your drawing. For one shape, write the name of an Indian or community festival that happens when the Moon is in that shape.
assessment_items.scaffold: Shape 1: Draw and name it. Shape 2: Draw and name it. Shape 3: Draw and name it. Shape 4: Draw and name it. For one shape, write: 'The festival _______ happens when the Moon looks like this.'
format_of_output: At least one festival linked to a Moon shape
assessment_items.annotation: Accept: full circle (Poornima), half-moon, crescent (C-shape), invisible/absent (Amavasya) as the four shapes — any four accurate phases qualify. For the festival link, accept any festival the child's community celebrates tied to any Moon phase, in any language. Regional variation note: festival names, languages, and associated Moon phases vary across India and the world — any correct pairing from the child's own community is fully valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe, name, and record repeating patterns in the appearance of celestial objects across different nights.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the child can recall and accurately represent the Moon's changing shapes across a lunar cycle and connect at least one phase to a cultural event in their community.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Four shapes should cover the range of phases — full, half, crescent, and absent. A child who draws four near-identical crescents has not grasped the variety of phases. The festival link is a one-line connection; it does not need to be explained, only correctly paired.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four visually distinct Moon shapes with accurate names (Poornima, half-moon, crescent, Amavasya or equivalent), festival correctly paired with the phase shape. Weak: fewer than four distinct shapes, shapes not named, no festival linked or festival linked to the wrong phase.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Children who have rarely seen the night sky may name phases from the class drawing activity or textbook — this is acceptable. Children who name phases in regional language equivalents (e.g., Purnima, Chaturthi) are fully credited.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled drawings with a written festival link
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing Moon phases is the core textbook task; adding a festival link integrates the natural and cultural strands the chapter develops together.

assessment_items.question_text: Many festivals in India and around the world are celebrated on specific Moon-phase nights — some on Poornima (full Moon), some on Amavasya (new Moon), and some on the first crescent. Why do you think people across many communities have chosen to connect festivals to the shape of the Moon? Give at least two reasons and support each with an example.
look_for: Acknowledgement that the Moon's changing shape is a visible, shared, natural signal that everyone can see without instruments
Recognition that the Moon provided an early way to count days and months, making it a natural basis for calendars and timing community events
At least one correctly paired festival-and-Moon-phase example (e.g., Diwali on Amavasya, Eid on first crescent, Rakshabandhan or Guru Poornima on Poornima)
Some sense that the Moon's reliability and regularity made it trustworthy for scheduling celebrations across generations
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for quality of reasoning, not number of festivals listed. A response that gives one well-reasoned explanation with a correct example earns more than one listing three festivals without reasoning. Regional variation note: any festival from any community or religion that is correctly linked to a Moon phase is valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a natural phenomenon's observable pattern and cultural practices in their community.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

Some sense that the Moon's reliability and regularity made it trustworthy for scheduling celebrations across generations

assessment_items.question_text: The Vikram Lander landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023 as part of India's Chandrayaan mission. Which of the following correctly describes ONE difference between day and night on Earth?

options.label: A
options.text: At night the Sun is in the sky but gives less light than during the day

options.label: B
options.text: Day and night are the same on the Moon as on Earth because both are lit by the Sun

options.label: C
options.text: During the day the Moon is visible; at night the Sun takes the Moon's place

options.label: D
options.text: During the day the Sun provides light and heat; at night the Sun is not visible and it is darker and cooler

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This is the core day/night difference from the chapter's comparison task. The question includes the Chandrayaan context to situate it in the section without requiring any knowledge beyond the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically compare two states of a natural phenomenon and describe how living things respond differently to each.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'the Sun is in the sky but gives less light at night' reveals a misconception that the Sun is present but dimmer at night — the student has not grasped that the Sun is not visible from a location during its night hours.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'during the day the Moon is visible and at night the Sun takes the Moon's place' indicates confusion between the Sun and Moon as alternating objects — the student has not separated the solar and lunar cycles.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'day and night are the same on the Moon as on Earth' shows the student is over-generalising from the chapter's Chandrayaan context without reasoning about the Moon's own rotation and lack of atmosphere — a plausible error after the Chandrayaan discussion.

assessment_items.question_text: Meera's teacher said: 'The Sun appears to move from East to West during the day.' Meera is curious and wants to ask questions. Write two questions Meera could ask her teacher about this statement. Then, in one sentence, explain why your shadow points in a different direction in the morning than in the afternoon when you stand in the same spot.
expected_elements: At least one question that probes the observed pattern (e.g., 'Does the Sun always rise in the East?', 'Why does the Sun seem to move — is it really the Sun that moves or is it something else?', 'Does the Sun's path change across seasons?')

At least one question that shows curiosity about cause or implication (e.g., 'If the Sun moves from East to West, does that mean shadows always point West in the morning?', 'Does the Sun follow the same path every day?')

An explanation connecting shadow direction change to the Sun's apparent position: that the shadow falls opposite to where the Sun is, so when the Sun is in the East (morning) the shadow points West, and when the Sun is in the West (afternoon) the shadow points East
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per element, up to three marks. Questions need not use scientific vocabulary — credit any question that genuinely probes the pattern or its cause. The shadow explanation must include the idea of opposition (shadow is opposite the Sun) to earn full credit for that element.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can formulate questions about an observed natural pattern and construct evidence-based explanations for the pattern's effects.

assessment_items.task: Write a short poem of four to eight lines about any part of the sky you find beautiful or interesting — the Sun, the Moon, the shadows, the stars, or the night sky. Your poem does not have to rhyme, but it should show something you truly noticed or felt about the sky.
assessment_items.scaffold: You may start with one of these opening lines if you like, or write your own: 'When the Sun rises over the rooftops…' / 'The Moon last night was shaped like…' / 'My shadow is longest when…' — then continue in your own words for four to eight lines.
format_of_output: A poem of four to eight lines
The poem may include a title
assessment_items.annotation: Do not assess literary quality or rhyme. Assess whether the poem draws on at least one accurate, specific observation or concept from the chapter (shadow length, Moon phase, star pattern, sky colour change, Sun's apparent path, cultural connection to sky objects). A poem that is beautiful but contains no traceable chapter content earns partial credit only. Regional variation note: poems written in any language are accepted; the teacher may ask the child to read it aloud if written in a script the teacher cannot read.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present understanding of natural phenomena and cultural connections through creative written and drawn expression.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the child can channel chapter learning into a creative piece that shows genuine personal observation or connection — demonstrating that understanding has been internalised, not just memorised.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold offers three optional opening lines covering shadows, Moon, and the Sun — each pointing to a chapter strand. Children who use none of these and start their own way are equally credited. Look for at least one specific, accurate sky detail, not just general beauty language.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: uses specific vocabulary from the chapter (Poornima, shadow, East, stars, crescent, Amavasya) in an image that shows the child understands what the word means; the poem reads as personal, not copied. Weak: generic 'the sky is beautiful and blue' with no specific chapter content; or a poem copied from a familiar source with no personalisation.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Accept poems in any Indian language or home language. Accept poems without rhyme. Accept poems that are only four lines if the four lines carry genuine content. A child who cannot write may dictate the poem to the teacher who writes it for them — the assessment is of the idea, not the handwriting.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook's own Let us reflect task asks for a sky-inspired poem — this OPEN_TASK directly assesses whether the child can produce that creative synthesis, which is the chapter's culminating expressive task.
